questions.q: The difference-of-squares trick computes 17 x 23 as 20^2 - 3^2. What makes this approach work?
options: 17 and 23 happen to both be prime numbers
17 and 23 are equidistant from the midpoint 20 (20-3 and 20+3), so their product equals m^2 - d^2 by algebra
It only works because 17 x 23 happens to equal 391 by coincidence
Any two integers can be multiplied this way regardless of their relationship
questions.explain: Writing the two numbers as (m-d) and (m+d) around a convenient midpoint m lets you use (m-d)(m+d) = m^2 - d^2, which only requires squaring a round number and a small number.

questions.q: The mental estimate sqrt(50) ~ 7 + 1/14 is derived from which Chapter 1 concept?
options: The chain rule for composite functions
A first-order (linear) Taylor approximation, f(a+h) ~ f(a) + f'(a)h, applied to f(x) = sqrt(x) around the perfect square a=49
Integration by substitution
The quotient rule for derivatives
questions.explain: Using f(x)=sqrt(x), f'(x)=1/(2 sqrt(x)), the linear approximation f(a+h) ~ f(a) + f'(a)h with a=49, h=1 gives sqrt(50) ~ 7 + 1/14, matching the actual value of about 7.0711 very closely.

questions.q: Why is 72 used in the 'Rule of 72' instead of the more mathematically exact constant 69.3 (100 * ln 2) for estimating doubling time under discrete compounding?
options: 72 is actually the mathematically exact constant and 69.3 is the approximation
72 has many more small integer divisors (2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12...), making mental division by common growth rates easier, at a small cost in accuracy
69.3 only works for negative growth rates
There is no difference between the two constants
questions.explain: 69.3 (from ln 2 ~ 0.693) is the more precise constant for continuous compounding, but 72 divides evenly by many more common rates (6%, 8%, 9%, 12%, etc.), making it more convenient for quick mental division while remaining reasonably accurate for typical rates.

questions.q: To estimate P(at least 60 heads in 100 fair coin flips) mentally, you note the mean is 50, the standard deviation is 5, and 60 is 2 standard deviations above the mean. What rule of thumb gives a quick estimate of this tail probability?
options: P(Z >= 2) is about 50%
P(Z >= 2) is about 2.5%, consistent with roughly 5% of a normal distribution lying beyond 2 standard deviations combined across both tails
P(Z >= 2) is about 0%, since 2 standard deviations is effectively impossible
P(Z >= 2) is about 95%
questions.explain: The empirical 68-95-99.7 rule says about 95% of a normal distribution lies within 2 standard deviations, leaving about 5% split between both tails, or roughly 2.5% in the upper tail alone — close to the exact binomial answer of about 2.8%.

questions.q: What is the common thread connecting all the mental-math techniques in this lesson?
options: They are unrelated tricks with no shared mathematical basis
Each technique is a compressed, fast application of an earlier course concept: algebraic identities, linear Taylor approximation, or the Central Limit Theorem
They all require memorizing large lookup tables
They only apply to numbers smaller than 100
questions.explain: Difference of squares is algebra, the square-root and compounding shortcuts are linear (first-order Taylor) approximations from Chapter 1, and the tail-probability estimate leans on the Central Limit Theorem from Chapter 3 — each trick is an earlier concept applied quickly.
